children.name: Anous
children.description: Noddies — dark-plumaged tropical terns with distinctive pale or white caps, breeding on tropical islands across all three major oceans. Unlike most terns, noddies do not plunge-dive but snatch prey from the surface, and they often rest on the sea rather than staying constantly airborne.

children.name: Anous albivitta
children.description: The grey noddy or grey ternlet (Anous albivitta) is a seabird belonging to the family Laridae..

children.name: Anous ceruleus
children.description: The blue noddy or hinaokū or manuohina (Anous ceruleus) is a seabird in the family Laridae..

children.name: Anous minutus
children.description: The black noddy (Anous minutus), also known as white-capped noddy, is a species of tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Anous stolidus
children.description: The brown noddy, common noddy or noddy tern (Anous stolidus) is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Anous tenuirostris
children.description: The lesser noddy (Anous tenuirostris), also known as the sooty noddy, is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Chlidonias
children.description: Marsh terns — dark-bodied freshwater terns that pick insects and small prey from the surface of marshes rather than plunge-diving.

children.name: Chlidonias niger
children.description: The black tern is a small tern generally found in or near inland water that breeds in Europe, Western Asia and North America. In winter the birds migrate to coastal areas of Africa and South America.

children.name: Chlidonias hybrida
children.description: The whiskered tern (Chlidonias hybrida) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Chlidonias leucopterus
children.description: The white-winged tern or white-winged black tern is a species of tern in the family Laridae. It is a small species generally found in or near bodies of fresh water across much of the world, including Europe, Africa, Asia, and Australia. The genus name is from Ancient Greek khelidonios, "swallow-like", from khelidon, "swallow".

children.name: Chlidonias albostriatus
children.description:
The black-fronted tern (Chlidonias albostriatus), sea martin, ploughboy, or tarapiroe, is a medium-small tern endemic to New Zealand. Black-fronted terns can be found in coastal habitats from the southern tip of the North Island to the eastern South Island as well as Stewart Island. Their breeding range is restricted to the South Island, where they will form breeding colonies on braided river islands.
The species is globally and nationally endangered, due to its small and declining national population. Black-fronted terns are vulnerable to a range of threats, including predation by introduced mammals, habitat loss (land use changes and weed encroachment), resource abstraction (gravel and water), human disturbance, and climate change.

children.name: Chroicocephalus
children.description: Hooded and black-headed gulls — smaller than Larus, characterised in summer by dark hoods that range from black to chocolate brown. The black-headed gull (skrattmås) is the most numerous gull in Stockholm and across Sweden's inland waters: its breeding colonies produce a cacophony of laughing calls that give it its Swedish name ('skratt' = laugh). Despite the name, the summer hood is actually dark chocolate brown, not black. Black-headed gulls are inland birds as much as coastal ones, following ploughs, roosting on city parks, and commuting between feeding areas and inland reservoirs in spectacular evening flights.

children.name: Chroicocephalus brunnicephalus
children.description:
The brown-headed gull (Chroicocephalus brunnicephalus) is a small gull which breeds in the high plateaus of central Asia from Tajikistan to Ordos in Inner Mongolia. It is migratory, wintering on the coasts and large inland lakes of the Indian subcontinent. As is the case with many gulls, was traditionally placed in the genus Larus.
This gull breeds in colonies in large reedbeds or marshes, or on islands in lakes, nesting on the ground. Like most gulls, it is highly gregarious in winter, both when feeding or in evening roosts. It is not a pelagic species, and is rarely seen at sea far from coasts.

children.name: Chroicocephalus bulleri
children.description: The black-billed gull (Chroicocephalus bulleri), also called Buller's gull or tarāpuka, is a Near Threatened species of gull in the family Laridae. This gull is found only in New Zealand, its ancestors having arrived from Australia around 250,000 years ago.

children.name: Chroicocephalus cirrocephalus
children.description: The grey-headed gull (Chroicocephalus cirrocephalus), also known as the grey-hooded gull, is a small species of gull which breeds patchily in South America and Africa south of the Sahara. It is not truly migratory, but is dispersive, becoming more widespread in winter. This species has occurred as a rare vagrant to the United States, Italy, and Spain. As is the case with many gulls, it had traditionally been placed in the genus Larus. Recent evidence suggests the South American and African populations may represent two separate cryptic species.

children.name: Chroicocephalus genei
children.description:
The slender-billed gull (Chroicocephalus genei) is a mid-sized gull which breeds very locally around the Mediterranean and the north of the western Indian Ocean (e.g. Pakistan) on islands and coastal lagoons. Most of the population is somewhat migratory, wintering further south to as far as North Africa and India. A few birds have wandered to western Europe. A vagrant individual was reportedly seen on Antigua, April 24, 1976 (AOU, 2000).
The genus name Chroicocephalus is from Ancient Greek khroizo, "to colour", and kephale, "head". The specific genei commemorates Italian naturalist Giuseppe Gené.

children.name: Chroicocephalus hartlaubii
children.description: Hartlaub's gull (Chroicocephalus hartlaubii) is a small gull in the genus Chroicocephalus..

children.name: Chroicocephalus maculipennis
children.description: The brown-hooded gull (Chroicocephalus maculipennis) is a species of gull, found in South America in Argentina, southeastern Brazil, Chile, Uruguay, and in the South Atlantic Ocean on the Falkland Islands. Its specific epithet, maculipennis, means 'spotted wings' (macula + penna). Like the other species of the genus Chroicocephalus, it was formerly included in a broad view of the genus Larus.

children.name: Chroicocephalus minutus
children.description: The world's smallest gull at just 28 cm. Black underwing and black hood in summer. Breeds in Scandinavian and Baltic marshes. Occurs regularly on passage along Swedish coasts. Has a delicate, tern-like flight, dipping to the surface to pick off insects.

children.name: Chroicocephalus novaehollandiae
children.description: The silver gull (Chroicocephalus novaehollandiae) is a gull in Oceania.

children.name: Chroicocephalus philadelphia
children.description: Bonaparte's gull (Chroicocephalus philadelphia) is a member of the gull family Laridae found mainly in northern North America. At in length, it is one of the smallest species of gull. Its plumage is mainly white with grey upperparts. During breeding season, Bonaparte's gull gains a slaty-black hood. The sexes are similar in appearance.

children.name: Chroicocephalus ridibundus
children.description: The black-headed gull is a small gull that breeds in much of the Palearctic in Europe and Asia, and also locally in smaller numbers in coastal eastern Canada. Most of the population is migratory and winters further south, but many also remain in the milder areas of northwestern Europe. It was formerly sometimes cited as "common black-headed gull" to distinguish it from "great black-headed gull".

children.name: Chroicocephalus saundersi
children.description: Saunders's gull (Saundersilarus saundersi) or Chinese black-headed gull, is a species of gull in the family Laridae..

children.name: Chroicocephalus serranus
children.description: The Andean gull (Chroicocephalus serranus) is a species in subfamily Larinae of the family Laridae, the gulls, terns, and skimmers.

children.name: Creagrus
children.description: Creagrus - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Creagrus furcatus
children.description: The swallow-tailed gull (Creagrus furcatus) is an equatorial seabird in the gull family, Laridae..

children.name: Feducciavis
children.description: Feducciavis - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Gaviota
children.description: Gaviota - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Gaviota niobrara
children.description: Gaviota niobrara is an extinct species of gull that lived during the Miocene..

children.name: Gelochelidon
children.description: Gull-billed terns — stout, short-billed terns that hawk insects and small vertebrates over land as well as water.

children.name: Gelochelidon macrotarsa
children.description: The Australian tern or Australian gull-billed tern (Gelochelidon macrotarsa) is a tern in the family Laridae, native to Australia..

children.name: Gelochelidon nilotica
children.description: The gull-billed tern (Gelochelidon nilotica) is a tern in the family Laridae. It is widely distributed and breeds in scattered localities in Europe, Asia, northwest Africa, and the Americas. The Australian gull-billed tern was previously considered a subspecies.

children.name: Gygis
children.description: White terns — ethereally beautiful, entirely snow-white tropical seabirds that famously lay their single egg on a bare branch with no nest. The large blue eye and translucent wings give them an otherworldly appearance.

children.name: Gygis alba
children.description: The Atlantic white tern (Gygis alba), also known as the common white tern, is a small seabird found in the Atlantic Ocean.

children.name: Gygis microrhyncha
children.description: The little white tern (Gygis microrhyncha) is a small seabird found in French Polynesia and the Republic of Kiribati. This species was previously considered a subspecies of the white tern (Gygis alba microrhyncha), but is now recognised as a separate species.

children.name: Hydrocoloeus
children.description: Hydrocoloeus - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Hydrocoloeus minutus
children.description: The little gull (Hydrocoloeus minutus) is a species of gull belonging to the family Laridae which is mainly found in the Palearctic with some small colonies in North America..

children.name: Hydroprogne
children.description: A monotypic genus for the Caspian tern, the largest tern in the world.

children.name: Hydroprogne caspia
children.description: The Caspian tern is the world's largest species of tern, with a subcosmopolitan but scattered distribution. Despite its extensive range, it is monotypic of its genus, and has no accepted subspecies. The genus name is from Ancient Greek hudro-, "water-", and Latin progne, "swallow".

children.name: Ichthyaetus
children.description: Large dark-hooded gulls of southern Eurasia and Africa, several with striking black or grey hoods in breeding plumage.

children.name: Ichthyaetus audouinii
children.description:
Audouin's gull (Ichthyaetus audouinii) is a large gull restricted to the Mediterranean and the western coast of Saharan Africa and the Iberian Peninsula. The genus name is from Ancient Greek ikhthus, "fish", and aetos, "eagle", and the specific audouinii and the English name are after the French naturalist Jean Victoire Audouin.
It breeds on small islands colonially or alone, laying 2–3 eggs on a ground nest. As is the case with many gulls, it has traditionally been placed in the genus Larus.

children.name: Ichthyaetus hemprichii
children.description: The sooty gull (Ichthyaetus hemprichii) is a species of gull in the family Laridae, also known as the Aden gull or Hemprich's gull.

children.name: Ichthyaetus ichthyaetus
children.description: Pallas's gull (Ichthyaetus ichthyaetus), also known as the great black-headed gull, is a large bird species. As is the case with many gulls, it has traditionally been placed in the genus Larus. The scientific name is from Ancient Greek. Ichthyaetus is from ikhthus, "fish", and aetos, "eagle".

children.name: Ichthyaetus leucophthalmus
children.description: The white-eyed gull (Ichthyaetus leucophthalmus) is a small gull that is endemic to the Red Sea. Its closest relative is the sooty gull. The species is classed as Least Concern by the IUCN; human pressure and oil pollution are deemed the major threats. As is the case with many gulls, it has traditionally been placed in the genus Larus.

children.name: Ichthyaetus melanocephalus
children.description: The Mediterranean gull (Ichthyaetus melanocephalus) is a small gull.

children.name: Ichthyaetus relictus
children.description: The relict gull or Central Asian gull (Ichthyaetus relictus) is a medium-sized gull.

children.name: Larosterna
children.description: A monotypic genus containing only the Inca tern, one of the most striking and unusual seabirds in the world, unique to the cold Humboldt Current system of the South American Pacific coast.

children.name: Larosterna inca
children.description: The Inca tern (Larosterna inca) is a near-threatened species of tern in the subfamily Sterninae of the family Laridae (the gulls, terns, and skimmers).

children.name: Larus
children.description: Large gulls — the dominant seabirds of northern European coastlines and the most familiar waterbirds in Swedish cities. Gulls are supremely opportunistic generalists: they eat fish, invertebrates, carrion, garbage, and other birds' eggs and chicks with equal facility. Their intelligence is remarkable — herring gulls have been documented dropping shellfish onto hard surfaces to break them open, and individuals can recognise specific human faces. Stockholm's rocky archipelago supports large colonies of herring gulls and lesser black-backed gulls, whose calls are the ambient soundtrack of the Swedish coast. 'Gull identification' has become one of birding's most obsessive niches, with hybrids, unusual ages, and rare visitors drawing dedicated specialists.

children.name: Larus argentatus
children.description: The European herring gull or simply herring gull is a large gull, up to 66 cm (26 in) long. It breeds throughout the northern and western coasts of Europe. Some European herring gulls, especially those resident in colder areas, migrate farther south in winter, but many are permanent residents, such as in Ireland, Britain, Iceland, or on the North Sea shores.

children.name: Larus armenicus
children.description: The Armenian gull (Larus armenicus) is a large gull found in the Caucasus and the Middle East.

children.name: Larus atlanticus
children.description: Olrog's gull (Larus atlanticus) is a species of gull found along the Atlantic coast of southern Brazil, Uruguay, and northern Argentina. It was formerly considered a subspecies of the very similar L. Belcheri. It is a large gull with a black back and wings, white head and underparts, a black band in the otherwise white tail, and a yellow bill with a red and black tip. Nonbreeding adults have a blackish head and a white eye ring. The species is named after Swedish-Argentine biologist Claes C. Olrog. It has a rather restricted breeding range and is threatened by habitat loss, and the IUCN has rated it as being "near threatened".

children.name: Larus barabensis
children.description: The lesser black-backed gull (Larus fuscus) is a large gull that breeds on the Atlantic and Arctic coasts of Europe.

children.name: Larus belcheri
children.description: Belcher's gull, also known as the band-tailed gull, is a bird in the family Laridae found along the Pacific coast of South America. It formerly included the very similar Olrog's gull as a subspecies, but that bird occurs on the Atlantic coast of South America and is now accepted as a separate species Larus atlanticus. Belcher's gull is a medium-sized gull with a blackish mantle, white head and underparts, a black band on the otherwise white tail, and a yellow bill with a red and black tip.

children.name: Larus brachyrhynchus
children.description: The short-billed gull (Larus brachyrhynchus) is a species of gull that breeds in northwestern North America. In North America, it was previously known as the mew gull, when it was considered conspecific with the palearctic common gull (Larus canus). Most authorities, including the American Ornithological Society in 2021, have split the two populations as distinct species.

children.name: Larus bulleri
children.description: The black-billed gull (Chroicocephalus bulleri), also called Buller's gull or tarāpuka (Māori), is a Near Threatened species of gull in the family Laridae..

children.name: Larus cachinnans
children.description: The Caspian gull is a large gull and a member of the herring and lesser black-backed gull complex. The scientific name is from Latin. Larus appears to have referred to a gull or other large seabird, and cachinnans means 'laughing', from cachinnare 'to laugh'.

children.name: Larus californicus
children.description: The California gull (Larus californicus) is a medium-sized gull, smaller on average than the herring gull, but larger on average than the ring-billed gull (though it may overlap in size with both).

children.name: Larus canus
children.description: The common gull is a gull that breeds in cool temperate regions of the Palearctic from Iceland and Scotland east to Kamchatka in the Russian Far East. Most common gulls migrate further south in winter, reaching the Mediterranean Sea, the southern Caspian Sea, and the seas around China and Japan; northwest European populations are at least partly resident. The closely related short-billed gull was formerly often included in this species, which was then sometimes known collectively as "mew gull".

children.name: Larus crassirostris
children.description: The black-tailed gull (Larus crassirostris) is a gull native to shorelines of East Asia.

children.name: Larus delawarensis
children.description: The ring-billed gull (Larus delawarensis) is a medium-sized gull native to North America, breeding in Canada and the northern Contiguous United States, and wintering mainly in the United States and northern Mexico. The genus name is from Latin Larus which appears to have referred to a gull or other large seabird. The specific delawarensis refers to the Delaware River.

children.name: Larus dominicanus
children.description: The kelp gull (Larus dominicanus), also known as the Dominican gull, is a gull that breeds on coasts and islands through much of the Southern Hemisphere.

children.name: Larus elmorei
children.description: Larus elmorei is an extinct species of gull that lived during the mid-Pliocene..

children.name: Larus fuscus
children.description: The lesser black-backed gull is a large gull that breeds on the Atlantic and Arctic coasts of Europe. It is migratory, wintering from the British Isles south to West Africa. However, it has increased dramatically in North America, especially along the east coast.

children.name: Larus glaucescens
children.description: The glaucous-winged gull (Larus glaucescens) is a large, white-headed gull. The genus name is from Latin Larus which appears to have referred to a gull or other large seabird. The specific glaucescens is Neo-Latin for "glaucous" from the Ancient Greek, glaukos, denoting the grey color of its wings.

children.name: Larus glaucodes
children.description: Syntype: ZMB 13462 skin, collected by Eduard Poeppig in 1827 – 1829 in Chile. Syntype: ZMB 13463 (Lichtenstein 1832, Nr. 73 sub “ Larus ”), skin, collected by Meyen in “ Maerz ” [= 1 – 15 Mar 1831; see below] in “ Chile ” [= bay of Valparaíso, Chile; see below]. For photos see Mallet-Rodriguez (2006: 177, fig. 3 – 4).

children.name: Larus glaucoides
children.description: The Iceland gull (Larus glaucoides) is a medium-sized gull that breeds in the Arctic regions of Canada and Greenland, but not in Iceland (as its name suggests), where it is only seen during winter.

children.name: Larus heermanni
children.description: Heermann's gull (Larus heermanni) is a gull resident in the United States, Mexico and extreme southwestern British Columbia, nearly all nesting on Isla Rasa in the Gulf of California. They are usually found near shores or well out to sea, very rarely inland. The species is named after Adolphus Lewis Heermann, nineteenth-century explorer and naturalist.

children.name: Larus heuglini
children.description: Heuglin's gull, or the Siberian gull (Larus fuscus heuglini), is a seabird in the genus Larus. It is sometimes considered as a separate species (Larus heuglini) but is usually treated as a subspecies of the lesser black-backed gull. Birds in the eastern part of Heuglin's gull's range are often paler grey above and sometimes considered to be a separate subspecies Larus fuscus taimyrensis (Taimyr gull). It is now thought that they are a result of hybridisation between Heuglin's gulls and Vega gulls.

children.name: Larus hyperboreus
children.description: The glaucous gull is a large gull, the second-largest gull in the world. The genus name is from Latin larus, which appears to have referred to a gull or other large seabird. The specific name hyperboreus is Latin for "northern" from the Ancient Greek Huperboreoi people from the far north "Glaucous" is from Latin glaucus and denotes the grey colour of the gull.

children.name: Larus kamtschatschensis
children.description: Bonaparte (1857: 224) listed " Gavina hinc Larus kamtschatschensis Bp. " in the synonymy of Larus niveus Pallas. The name is thus not available for nomenclatural purposes (Art. 11.6 of the Code) and the provisions of Art. 11.6.1 of the Code do not apply, because the name was already published in earlier works (Bonaparte 1855: 16, 1856: 771). In spite of this, Bonaparte's (1857) kamtschatschensis was used as a valid name for the taxon in recent literature (see above for citations), probably following Peters (1934: 315, footnote) who argued that “ a quotation [of a name in the synonymy of an available name] ipso facto renders the name a substitute name for the species in whose synonymy it is quoted. His argument does not match provisions of the Code (ICZN 1999).

children.name: Larus lacus
children.description: Larus lacus is an extinct species of gull that lived in North America during the Late Pliocene..

children.name: Larus livens
children.description: The yellow-footed gull (Larus livens) is a large gull, closely related to the western gull and thought to be a subspecies until the 1960s. It is endemic to the Gulf of California.

children.name: Larus marinus
children.description: The great black-backed gull (Larus marinus) is the largest member of the gull and tern family Laridae.

children.name: Larus michahellis
children.description: The yellow-legged gull or western yellow-legged gull is a large gull found in Europe, the Middle East and North Africa, which has only recently achieved wide recognition as a distinct species. It was formerly treated as a subspecies of either the Caspian gull L. cachinnans, or more broadly as a subspecies of the herring gull L.

children.name: Larus naumanni
children.description: A large, pale-mantled gull of Mongolian and Chinese plateau lakes, closely allied to the yellow-legged gull complex. Breeds on high-altitude inland lakes across Mongolia and adjacent China, and winters along the coasts of eastern China and Korea. Only recently widely accepted as a full species separate from the Caspian gull, following genetic analysis.

children.name: Larus occidentalis
children.description: The western gull (Larus occidentalis) is a large white-headed gull that lives on the west coast of North America and the Pacific Ocean.

children.name: Larus oregonus
children.description: Larus oregonus is an extinct species of gull that lived during the Late Pleistocene..

children.name: Larus pacificus
children.description: The Pacific gull (Larus pacificus) is a gull, native to the coasts of Australia.

children.name: Larus perpetuus
children.description: Larus perpetuus is an extinct species of gull that lived in North America during the Pliocene..

children.name: Larus robustus
children.description: Larus robustus is an extinct species of gull that lived during the Late Pleistocene..

children.name: Larus schistisagus
children.description: The slaty-backed gull (Larus schistisagus) is a large, white-headed gull that breeds on the north-eastern coast of the Palearctic, but travels widely during nonbreeding seasons. It is similar in appearance to the western gull and the glaucous-winged gull. Another alternate name is Pacific gull, though it also applies to a Southern Hemisphere species, L. Pacificus.

children.name: Larus smithsonianus
children.description:
The American herring gull (Larus smithsonianus or Larus argentatus smithsonianus), also known as the Arctic herring gull or Smithsonian gull, is a large gull that breeds in North America, where it is treated by the American Ornithological Society as a subspecies of herring gull (L. Argentatus).
Adults are white with gray back and wings, black wingtips with white spots, and pink legs. Immature birds are gray-brown and are darker and more uniform than European herring gulls, with a darker tail. As is common with other gulls, they are colloquially referred to simply as seagulls.

children.name: Larus thayeri
children.description:
Thayer's gull (Larus glaucoides thayeri) is a subspecies of the Iceland gull. It is a large gull native to North America.
Somewhat intermediate between American herring gull and Iceland gull in habit and appearance and at times considered conspecific with either species, the adult Thayer's gull in nonbreeding plumage has a pale gray mantle, with obvious blackish wingtips, and extensive brown streaking on the head and neck. The head, neck, breast, belly, and underwings are primarily white, and the legs are pink. There is a red spot on the lower mandible, and the color of the iris is generally dark. In summer, the head and neck are white, with the bill turning bright yellow with a larger red spot on the lower mandible. Juvenile gulls are brown, with black bills, and black legs which quickly fade to adult pink. Thayer's Gull reaches a length, with a wingspan of and a weight of approximately. Males average around and females, being slightly smaller, average. Among standard measurements, the wing chord is, the bill is and the tarsus is.

children.name: Larus utunui
children.description: The Huahine gull (Chroicocephalus utunui), also known as the Society Islands gull, is an extinct bird, a species of gull of which subfossil bones were found at the Fa'ahia archeological site on Huahine, in the Society Islands of French Polynesia..

children.name: Larus vegae
children.description: The Vega gull, East Siberian gull, or East Siberian herring gull (Larus vegae) is a large gull of the herring gull/lesser black-backed gull complex which breeds in Northeast Asia.

children.name: Leucophaeus
children.description: American hooded gulls including the abundant laughing gull and the desert-nesting grey gull.

children.name: Leucophaeus atricilla
children.description: The laughing gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) is a medium-sized gull of North and South America.

children.name: Leucophaeus modestus
children.description: The grey gull, also known as garuma gull (Leucophaeus modestus), is a medium-sized gull native to South America.

children.name: Leucophaeus fuliginosus
children.description: The lava gull (Leucophaeus fuliginosus), also known as the dusky gull, and is the rarest gull in the world.

children.name: Leucophaeus pipixcan
children.description: Franklin's gull (Leucophaeus pipixcan) is a small gull. The genus name Leucophaeus is from Ancient Greek leukos, "white", and phaios, "dusky". The specific pipixcan is a Nahuatl name for a type of gull. The English common name was given to commemorate the arctic explorer Sir John Franklin, who led an expedition in 1825 on which the type was collected.

children.name: Leucophaeus scoresbii
children.description: The dolphin gull (Leucophaeus scoresbii), sometimes erroneously called the red-billed gull (a somewhat similar but unrelated species from New Zealand), is a gull native to southern Chile and Argentina, and the Falkland Islands.

children.name: Onychoprion
children.description: Tropical seabird terns with dark upperparts that spend years continuously at sea before returning to breed on remote islands.

children.name: Onychoprion fuscatus
children.description: The sooty tern (Onychoprion fuscatus) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Onychoprion aleuticus
children.description: The Aleutian tern is a migratory bird living in the subarctic region of the globe most of the year. It is frequently associated with the Arctic tern, which it closely resembles. While both species have a black cap, the Aleutian tern may be distinguished by its white forehead.

children.name: Onychoprion anaethetus
children.description: The bridled tern (Onychoprion anaethetus) is a seabird of the family Laridae.

children.name: Onychoprion lunatus
children.description: The spectacled tern (Onychoprion lunatus), also known as the grey-backed tern, is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Pagophila
children.description: A monotypic genus for the ivory gull, the only entirely white gull, tied to the high Arctic pack ice.

children.name: Pagophila eburnea
children.description: The ivory gull (Pagophila eburnea) is a small gull, the only species in the genus Pagophila.

children.name: Phaetusa
children.description: Phaetusa - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Phaetusa simplex
children.description: The large-billed tern (Phaetusa simplex) is a species of tern in the family Laridae..

children.name: Procelsterna
children.description: Blue noddies — tiny, pale terns of the tropical Pacific, the most delicate members of the Laridae, feeding on zooplankton and tiny fish by dipping to the sea surface.

children.name: Procelsterna cerulea
children.description: The blue noddy or hinaokū or manuohina (Anous ceruleus) is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Pseudosterna
children.description: Pseudosterna - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Rhodostethia
children.description: Rhodostethia - a genus in the family Laridae.

children.name: Rhodostethia rosea
children.description: Ross's gull (Rhodostethia rosea) is a small gull, the only species in its genus, although it has been suggested the genus should be merged with the closely related Hydrocoloeus, which otherwise only includes the little gull..

children.name: Rissa
children.description: Kittiwakes — small, gentle, truly pelagic gulls that nest on sheer sea cliffs and spend the rest of the year far out at sea.

children.name: Rissa brevirostris
children.description: The red-legged kittiwake (Rissa brevirostris) is a seabird species in the gull family Laridae. It breeds in the Pribilof Islands, Bogoslof Island, and Buldir Island in the Bering Sea off the coast of Alaska, and the Commander Islands, Russia, and spends the winter at sea.

children.name: Rissa estesi
children.description: Rissa estesi is an extinct species of bird in the genus Rissa that lived during the Piacenzian stage of the Neogene period..

children.name: Rissa tridactyla
children.description: The black-legged kittiwake is a seabird species in the gull family Laridae. This species was first described by Carl Linnaeus in his landmark 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae as Larus tridactylus. The English name is derived from its call, a shrill 'kittee-wa-aaake, kitte-wa-aaake'.

children.name: Rynchops
children.description: Skimmers — unique terns with a lower mandible longer than the upper, used to slice through the water surface in flight to snap up fish.

children.name: Rynchops albicollis
children.description: The Indian skimmer (Rynchops albicollis) or Indian scissors-bill, is one of the three species that belong to the skimmer genus Rynchops in the family Laridae.

children.name: Rynchops flavirostris
children.description: The African skimmer is a species of bird belonging to the skimmer genus Rynchops in the family Laridae. It is found along rivers, lakes and lagoons in Sub-Saharan Africa.

children.name: Rynchops niger
children.description: The black skimmer (Rynchops niger) is a tern-like seabird, one of three similar bird species in the skimmer genus Rynchops in the gull family Laridae.

children.name: Sterna
children.description: Sea terns — elegant, sharply pointed seabirds built for plunge-diving into the sea for small fish. Terns are the migrants par excellence: the Arctic tern (silvertärna) makes the longest migration of any animal on Earth, breeding in the Arctic (including northern Sweden's coast) and wintering in the Antarctic, covering 70,000–90,000 km annually — it experiences more daylight than any other creature. Common terns (fisktärna) breed in noisy, fiercely defensive colonies on Swedish coastal rocks and lake islands. Terns dive at speed into the water to catch fish, folding their wings at the last moment. Their aggressive colony defence — dive-bombing and occasionally striking intruders — makes tern colonies an exciting experience for visiting naturalists.

children.name: Sterna acuticauda
children.description:
The black-bellied tern (Sterna acuticauda) is a tern found near large rivers in the Indian subcontinent, its range extending from Pakistan, Nepal and India to Myanmar. It has become very scarce in the eastern part of its range and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has assessed its conservation status as being endangered.
They have a black belly in the summer and a deep forked tail. They can sometimes resemble whiskered terns (Chlidonias hybrida), but the deeper fork of the tail and the black on the lower belly distinguish them from the shallow fork and black closer to the breast on the whiskered tern. Considering that sequence analysis supports moving the similar black-fronted tern ("Sterna" albostriata) into Chlidonias, this species might also be better placed in that genus, but no research has yet been conducted.

children.name: Sterna aurantia
children.description: , Karnataka]] The river tern or Indian river tern (Sterna aurantia) is a tern in the family Laridae, the largest species currently included in the genus Sterna of typical terns.

children.name: Sterna dougallii
children.description: The roseate tern (Sterna dougallii) is a species of tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Sterna forsteri
children.description:
Forster's tern (Sterna forsteri) is a tern in the family Laridae. The genus name Sterna is derived from Old English "stearn", "tern", and forsteri commemorates the naturalist Johann Reinhold Forster.
It breeds inland in North America in the northern United States and southern Canada, and migrates south to winter in the southern United States, Mexico, the Caribbean, and northern Central America. It is also a rare but annual vagrant in western Europe, and has wintered in Ireland and Great Britain on a number of occasions.

children.name: Sterna hirundinacea
children.description: The South American tern (Sterna hirundinacea) is a species of tern found in coastal regions of southern South America, including the Falkland Islands, ranging north to Peru (Pacific coast) and Brazil (Atlantic coast)..

children.name: Sterna hirundo
children.description: The common tern is a seabird in the family Laridae. This bird has a circumpolar distribution, its four subspecies breeding in temperate and subarctic regions of Europe, Asia and North America. It is strongly migratory, wintering in coastal tropical and subtropical regions.

children.name: Sterna paradisaea
children.description: The Arctic tern is a tern in the family Laridae. This bird has a circumpolar breeding distribution covering the Arctic and subarctic regions of Europe, Asia, and North America. The species is strongly migratory, seeing two summers each year as it migrates along a convoluted route from its northern breeding grounds to the Antarctic coast for the southern summer and back again about six months later.

children.name: Sterna repressa
children.description: The white-cheeked tern (Sterna repressa) is a species of tern in the family Laridae. It is found around the coasts on the Red Sea, around the Horn of Africa to Kenya, in the Persian Gulf and along the Iranian coast to Pakistan and western India.

children.name: Sterna sandvicensis
children.description: The Sandwich tern (Thalasseus sandvicensis) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Sterna striata
children.description:
The white-fronted tern (Sterna striata), also known as tara, sea swallow, black-billed tern, kahawai bird, southern tern, or swallow tail, was first described by Johann Friedrich Gmelin in 1789. A medium-sized tern with an all-white body including underwing and forked tail, with pale grey hues on the mantle and upper side of the wing. In breeding adults a striking black cap covers the head from forehead to nape, leaving a small white strip above the black bill.
This is the most abundant tern in New Zealand. It can be observed feeding on shoaling fish along the entire coastline and many of the smaller outlying islands. Breeding occurs from October to January on rocky cliffs, offshore islands and along the coast where pairs will nest on shingle, sand, shell or rock. Flocks may contain hundreds of breeding pairs that will nest in close proximity to one another. Large numbers of juveniles and some adults migrate to the south-east coast of Australia and parts of Tasmania in the autumn, with small numbers establishing breeding colonies on Flinders and Cape Barren Islands in the Bass Strait.

children.name: Sterna sumatrana
children.description: The black-naped tern (Sterna sumatrana) is an oceanic tern mostly found in tropical and subtropical areas of the Indian Ocean and western Pacific Ocean. They are rarely found inland. It was described from the islands around Sumatra. It is most closely related to roseate tern S. Dougallii and white-fronted tern S. Striata.

children.name: Sterna trudeaui
children.description: The snowy-crowned tern (Sterna trudeaui), also known as Trudeau's tern, is a species of bird in subfamily Sterninae of the family Laridae, the gulls, terns, and skimmers..

children.name: Sterna virgata
children.description: The Kerguelen tern (Sterna virgata) is a tern of the Southern Hemisphere..

children.name: Sterna vittata
children.description: The Antarctic tern (Sterna vittata) is a seabird in the family Laridae.

children.name: Sternula
children.description: The smallest terns — fast-flying, yellow-billed species that hover and plunge into shallow water for tiny fish.

children.name: Sternula albifrons
children.description: The little tern (Sternula albifrons) is a seabird of the family Laridae.

children.name: Sternula antillarum
children.description: The least tern (Sternula antillarum) is a species of tern that breeds in North America and locally in northern South America.

children.name: Sternula balaenarum
children.description: The Damara tern (Sternula balaenarum) is a species of small tern in the family Laridae which breeds in the southern summer in southern Africa and migrates to tropical African coasts to winter.

children.name: Sternula lorata
children.description: The Peruvian tern (Sternula lorata) is a species of tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Sternula nereis
children.description: The fairy tern (Sternula nereis) is a small tern which is native to the southwestern Pacific.

children.name: Sternula saundersi
children.description:
Saunders's tern (Sternula saundersi), sometimes known as the black-shafted tern, is a species of bird in the family Laridae. It is sparsely resident along the shores of the north-western Indian Ocean (namely southern Somalia, Arabian Peninsula, Socotra, Pakistan, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and northern Sri Lanka).
It is a close relative of the little tern, least tern, yellow-billed tern, and Peruvian tern. In non-breeding plumages, the Saunder's tern and the little tern may be almost indistinguishable. The two have been considered by some to be conspecific.

children.name: Sternula sinensis
children.description: A critically endangered small tern breeding on a tiny number of sandy beaches in China, Taiwan, and the Philippines. The global population is estimated at just a few thousand birds and has been severely impacted by coastal development. Conservation efforts in Taiwan using artificial nesting platforms have produced encouraging results.

children.name: Sternula superciliaris
children.description: The yellow-billed tern (Sternula superciliaris) is a small seabird found in South America. It is a species of tern in the family Laridae. It is found in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, French Guiana, Guyana, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, Uruguay, and Venezuela. Its natural habitats are rivers, swamps, and freshwater lakes.

children.name: Thalasseus
children.description: Crested terns — large terns with shaggy black crests and slender bills, plunge-diving for fish in warm and temperate seas.

children.name: Thalasseus acuflavidus
children.description: Cabot's tern (Thalasseus acuflavidus) is a species of bird in subfamily Sterninae of the family Laridae, the gulls, terns, and skimmers. It is found on the coasts of the eastern United States and Middle America, the Caribbean, Trinidad and Tobago, and in every mainland South American country except landlocked Bolivia and Paraguay, though rare in Chile. It is also a vagrant in eastern Canada and western Europe.

children.name: Thalasseus albididorsalis
children.description: The West African crested tern (Thalasseus albididorsalis) is a bird species in the family Laridae..

children.name: Thalasseus bengalensis
children.description: The lesser crested tern (Thalasseus bengalensis) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Thalasseus bergii
children.description: The greater crested tern (Thalasseus bergii), also called crested tern, swift tern, or great crested tern, is a tern in the family Laridae that nests in dense colonies on coastlines and islands in the tropical and subtropical Old World.

children.name: Thalasseus bernsteini
children.description: The Chinese crested tern (Thalasseus bernsteini) is a tern in the family Laridae..

children.name: Thalasseus elegans
children.description: The elegant tern (Thalasseus elegans) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Thalasseus maximus
children.description: The royal tern (Thalasseus maximus) is a tern in the family Laridae.

children.name: Thalasseus sandvicensis
children.description: The Sandwich tern is a tern in the family Laridae. It is very closely related to the lesser crested tern, Chinese crested tern, Cabot's tern, and elegant tern and has been known to interbreed with both elegant and lesser crested terns. It breeds in the Palearctic from Europe to the Caspian Sea, and winters in the Mediterranean and on the coasts of Africa, India, and Sri Lanka.

children.name: Thalasseus zimmermanni
children.description: One of the world's rarest birds — fewer than 100 individuals are known to exist — breeding only on a handful of rocky islands off China and Taiwan. Distinguished from the greater crested tern by its yellow bill with a black tip and white-based black crest. Rediscovered breeding in 2000 after 63 years without confirmed records; listed as Critically Endangered.

children.name: Xema
children.description: A monotypic genus for Sabine's gull, a small, tern-like Arctic gull with a boldly patterned wing.

children.name: Xema sabini
children.description: Sabine's gull (SAY-bine or SAB-ine) (Xema sabini) is a small gull. It is usually treated as the only species placed in the genus Xema, though some authors include it with other gulls in a wide view of the genus Larus. It has also been known historically as fork-tailed gull or xeme (from the genus name). It breeds in colonies on Arctic coasts and tundra, laying two or three spotted olive-brown eggs in a ground nest lined with grass. Sabine's gull is pelagic outside the breeding season. It takes a wide variety of mainly animal food, and will eat any suitable small prey.
